title: Maximum-pair matching kept the larger-first share near 60.5% in shallow ComCat pairs in 2013-2025
abstract: We tested whether a global pair assignment changes earthquake size order measured with disjoint pairs. We used a fixed ComCat snapshot with shallow M5.5+ events. Pairs were 1 to below 30 days apart, within 200 km in three dimensions, and at least 0.5 magnitude units apart. In 2013-2025, shortest-gap greedy matching gave 256 larger-first pairs out of 423 (60.52%). Maximum-cardinality matching with minimum total time gap gave 268 out of 443 (60.50%). The paired difference was -0.02 percentage points. Its conditional 95% graph-bootstrap interval was -2.01 to +1.75 points. Thus the main size-order result changed little despite 20 added pairs. In 2000-2012, the difference was -1.15 points, with limits of -3.27 to +0.72. Some secondary settings had clear marginal changes. This extends prior filter-order work with a global matching test. It does not establish that the methods are equal or that pairs are caused aftershocks. Catalog revision, mixed magnitude types, fixed rules and group independence assumptions limit inference. Code, aggregate counts, two solver checks, scalar audits and a figure are included. External event records remain outside the baseline package.

display.caption: Left: larger-first shares under greedy and maximum-pair matching. Right: paired method differences in 2013-2025. Bars show conditional 95% graph-bootstrap intervals. These are marginal intervals, not simultaneous limits.

citations.reason: Prior filter-order comparison supplies the question and the same shared source snapshot. Our greedy counts reproduce its filter-first counts. This is not independent data.
Prior count-cancellation benchmark explains why pair selection must be explicit.
